2078000488.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The caecum is the blind-ended intestinal pouch situated in the right iliac fossa inferior to the ileocecal junction. It is characterized by three distinct taeniae coli converging at the posteromedial base of the vermiform appendix, sacculations (haustrations), and complete peritoneal covering without a true mesentery.
2078000488.keyConcept: The caecum occupies the right iliac fossa below the ileocecal opening and serves as the convergence point for all three taeniae coli at the appendiceal base.

747200626.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The ascending colon is the secondarily retroperitoneal segment of the large intestine extending vertically upward through the right flank and right lumbar region from the caecum to the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, continuing into the right colic flexure.
747200626.keyConcept: The ascending colon is fixed to the posterior abdominal wall (secondarily retroperitoneal) and ascends from the caecum to the hepatic flexure.

1028369543.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The sigmoid colon is the mobile, S-shaped intraperitoneal loop of large bowel suspended by the fan-shaped sigmoid mesocolon, extending from the pelvic brim (in continuation with the descending colon) to the third sacral vertebra (S3), where it terminates at the rectum.
1028369543.keyConcept: The sigmoid colon is an intraperitoneal loop with a distinct mesentery and numerous appendices epiploicae, transitioning into the rectum at the level of S3.

1410991567.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The right colic (hepatic) flexure is the acute right-angled bend connecting the ascending colon to the transverse colon in the right hypochondrium. It lies directly inferior to the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver (producing the colic impression) and anterior to the lower pole of the right kidney, positioned inferior to the left colic flexure.
1410991567.keyConcept: The right colic flexure marks the transition from ascending to transverse colon beneath the right lobe of the liver and lies lower than the splenic flexure.

1358738278.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The transverse colon is the longest and most mobile intraperitoneal segment of the large intestine, spanning horizontally across the abdomen from the right colic flexure to the left colic flexure, completely suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by the transverse mesocolon.
1358738278.keyConcept: The transverse colon crosses the abdominal cavity suspended by the transverse mesocolon and receives dual arterial supply from both the SMA and IMA.

1016081717.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The left colic (splenic) flexure is the sharp junction between the transverse colon and descending colon in the left hypochondrium. It lies against the visceral surface of the spleen and lower pole of the left kidney, anchored securely to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament and positioned higher and more posterior than the right colic flexure.
1016081717.keyConcept: The left colic (splenic) flexure is situated higher and more posteriorly than the hepatic flexure, supported by the phrenicocolic ligament.

1926563457.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The descending colon is the secondarily retroperitoneal segment of the large intestine passing vertically downward along the left posterior abdominal wall from the left colic flexure to the pelvic inlet, where it curves medially to become the sigmoid colon.
1926563457.keyConcept: The descending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal, narrower in caliber than the ascending colon, and supplied primarily by the left colic artery from the IMA.

1360952457.target: Atypical L5 vertebra as it short, thick, attached to pedicle & body
1360952457.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The atypical fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) is characterized by very massive, short, thick, conical/pyramidal transverse processes that are attached to both the pedicle and the lateral surface of the vertebral body, and by a large vertebral body with greater anterior than posterior vertical height.
1360952457.keyConcept: L5 is an atypical lumbar vertebra distinguished by its massive transverse processes attached continuously across both the pedicle and the vertebral body.

228256195.target: Typical L4 vertebra as it long, thin, attached to pedicle
228256195.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) feature long, thin, slender, horizontally directed transverse processes that arise solely from the junction of the pedicle and lamina (without any attachment to the vertebral body), a large kidney-shaped body, and a triangular vertebral foramen.
228256195.keyConcept: Typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) are recognized by slender transverse processes attached strictly to the neural arch/pedicle junction rather than the body.

197200429.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The specimen exhibits all hallmarks of typical lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4), including a reniform (kidney-shaped) body, triangular vertebral foramen, slender elongated transverse processes originating at the junction of pedicles and laminae, vertically oriented articular facets, and a horizontal hatchet-shaped spinous process.
197200429.keyConcept: Lumbar vertebrae L1 through L4 are typical lumbar vertebrae, whereas L5 is an atypical vertebra.

706229427.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrow indicates the pedicle of a typical lumbar vertebra, which is a short, stout, cylindrical bar of bone projecting straight posteriorly from the upper portion of the posterolateral aspect of the kidney-shaped vertebral body.
706229427.keyConcept: The pedicles of typical lumbar vertebrae are strong, short bony struts that form the lateral boundaries of the triangular vertebral foramen.

362561551.target: Short, thick pyramidal, attached to both pedicle & body
362561551.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrows point to the transverse processes of the atypical L5 vertebra, which are characteristically short, thick, and pyramidal in shape, and firmly anchored to both the pedicle and the lateral surface of the vertebral body to resist anterior shear forces and transmit load to the pelvis.
362561551.keyConcept: The transverse process of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) is uniquely short, thick, pyramidal, and attached to both the pedicle and vertebral body.

1002555422.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The symbols mark the central opening (vertebral foramen) within the vertebra, which is distinctly triangular in the lumbar region and contributes to the continuous vertebral canal housing the cauda equina, filum terminale, and spinal meninges.
1002555422.keyConcept: The lumbar vertebral foramen is triangular in cross-section and forms the vertebral canal that transmits the cauda equina.

672635931.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the mammillary process, a distinct rounded tubercle situated on the posterior margin of the superior articular process of a lumbar vertebra, serving as an attachment site for deep back muscles (multifidus and medial intertransversarii).
672635931.keyConcept: The mammillary process is a characteristic anatomical feature of lumbar vertebrae located on the posterior border of each superior articular process.

2114372962.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow points to the accessory process, a small bony projection found on the posterior aspect of the base (root) of the transverse process in lumbar vertebrae, serving as an insertion point for the intertransversarii and longissimus muscles.
2114372962.keyConcept: The accessory process is located on the posterior aspect of the root of the transverse process, distinguishing it from the mammillary process on the superior articular process.

1146392575.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows indicate the smooth, concave articular facet on the superior articular process of the lumbar vertebra, which is vertically oriented and faces medially and slightly posteriorly in the sagittal plane to interlock with the inferior articular facet of the superior adjacent vertebra.
1146392575.keyConcept: Lumbar superior articular facets are vertically oriented, concave, and face posteromedially to resist rotation while allowing flexion and extension.

1075328816.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The red arrow in this lateral view of articulated lumbar vertebrae points to the inferior articular facet, which projects downward from the junction of the pedicle and lamina and presents a smooth, convex articular surface directed anterolaterally.
1075328816.keyConcept: Lumbar inferior articular facets project inferiorly and face anterolaterally, fitting between the medially facing superior articular facets of the vertebra below.

832368195.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the spinous process (spine) of the lumbar vertebra, which is a broad, sturdy, quadrilateral (hatchet-shaped) plate of bone projecting horizontally backward from the junction of the two laminae in the posterior midline.
832368195.keyConcept: The lumbar spinous process is stout, horizontally directed, and quadrilateral, facilitating dorsal access to the vertebral canal for lumbar punctures.

1257203977.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the vertebral lamina, a broad, thick, flattened plate of bone extending posteromedially from the pedicle and articular processes to unite in the midline with its fellow from the opposite side, forming the posterior wall of the vertebral canal and the base of the spinous process.
1257203977.keyConcept: The lumbar laminae are broad, robust bony plates forming the posterior arch of the vertebra and serving as attachment sites for the ligamentum flavum.

356260245.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The arrows point to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, which project laterally from the vertebral arch (slender and elongated in typical vertebrae; thick and conical in atypical L5), functioning as leverage arms for muscular and ligamentous attachments.
356260245.keyConcept: Lumbar transverse processes represent costal elements projecting laterally from the junction of the pedicle and lamina (or pedicle and body in L5).
